The "two wrongs don't make a right" assertion all over this thread is never accompanied with an explanation of why that's important. Our society's insistence on human rights is designed to make each of us desire the continuance and stability of this particular society. It is in the interest of society and each individual who does buy into this to remove people who do not share that point of view, e.g. people who violate others' human rights, from society. By extension, this may also remove the human rights that the society they're being removed from insures for its members, and this is not wrong from that society's point of view. The reason it's not super quick and capricious is that it would make other members of society uneasy, and less secure in their continued membership which bodes ill for the society's long-term stability.

This notion of a society having rules that everybody mutually agrees to abide by as a requirement for membership in society and to reap the benefits of living in a society, is called the "social contract."

/u/dugite-code has the best answer so far: that it is very hard to prove beyond a shadow of doubt that somebody is in fact guilty. Up until that conviction, you must assume the person is still innocent, and therefore still entitled to their full human rights.

Incidentally, when proven beyond a shadow of a doubt, several (though fewer every year) U.S. states will put convicted murderers to death. This is explicitly taking away one of their human rights (life), but only after an extremely long process designed to be as sure as humanly possible that the person is in fact not innocent. One could also argue that imprisonment also infringes a human right - liberty.

TL;DR they don't (at least not all of them) but in real life, unlike works of fiction, we don't get to see all sides of the events and we don't get to know everyone's motivations so it is much more difficult to be provably, justifiably certain that somebody is in fact a murderer or otherwise unwilling to honor the social contract.

Sometimes we do take all human rights away from murderers. There are approximately 3,000 people of death row as we speak. A person was executed on last Thursday in Texas.
